# How to use Kling AI video templates in Picsart Flow

> **In short:** Picsart Flow includes Kling-powered video templates that turn a still photo, a character reference image, or a short script-plus-footage combo into a short AI-generated clip. You can try them without editing experience, though longer videos and higher resolution usually need a paid plan.

Want to make a short video but don't have filming skills, a camera, or editing software? Kling is a video-generation model that creates short clips from a still photo, a character image, or a written script combined with your existing footage. Picsart Flow hosts it as ready-made templates, so you mostly just upload, type a sentence, and wait. This guide walks through all three template styles one at a time. None of this requires a video background — only a clear idea of what kind of clip you'd like to end up with.

## Before you start

- A free Picsart account (you can sign up with email, Apple, or Google — check the latest sign-up options on the Picsart login page).
- The Picsart app on your phone, or the Picsart web editor on a laptop. Picsart Flow tools may live in different spots in each, so this guide uses language like "look for" rather than exact menu names.
- A few source images saved to your device. For best results, use clear, well-lit photos where the subject is centered.
- Around 15–30 minutes for your first full run-through (most of that is waiting for the AI to render).
- A realistic expectation: AI video is impressive but imperfect. People may look slightly off, hands can blur, and motion can wobble — that's normal for current tools.

## Step 1 — Open Picsart Flow and find the Kling templates

Tap the Picsart app to open it, then look along the bottom or side menu for a section called something like **Flow**, **AI Tools**, or **Video**. The exact label depends on your version and platform, so if you don't see "Flow", search inside the app for "Kling" or "AI video" — that usually leads you to the same area. Once you land on the Kling page, scroll until you see a row of template tiles. You'll typically find three styles: one that animates a single photo, one built around a character reference image, and one that combines your footage with a script.

💬 Example: search terms to try inside the app — `Kling`, `AI video`, `photo to video`.

You'll know it worked when you see a screen with several preview tiles, each labeled with the input it needs (photo, image, or footage).

## Step 2 — Use the photo-to-video template

Pick the **photo-to-video** template and tap it. The app will ask you to upload one image from your camera roll. Choose a clear photo where the main subject (a person, a pet, a product) is easy to see. After upload, a small text box appears asking what should happen in the video — that's called a **prompt** (the instruction you give the AI). Type one short sentence describing the motion you want, then tap the generate button. The app will show a progress indicator while Kling works. This step usually takes 30 seconds to a few minutes, depending on clip length and server load.

💬 Example: `The woman slowly turns her head to the right and smiles, with soft sunlight on her face.`

You'll know it worked when a short video preview appears in place of the still photo. If it looks wrong, tap regenerate or tweak the prompt — small wording changes make a big difference.

## Step 3 — Try the character reference sheet template

Now pick the **character reference** template, sometimes labeled "character sheet" or "consistent character." This one is designed for keeping the same face or outfit across multiple clips — useful for short stories, social media series, or product mascots. The app will ask you to upload one or more images of the same character from different angles. Add a short prompt describing the scene, then generate. Kling tries to keep facial features and clothing consistent, which is harder than it sounds for AI, so your first result may need two or three tries.

💬 Example: `A young woman with short black hair, wearing a yellow raincoat, walks through a misty forest at dawn.`

You'll know it worked when the generated clip shows a person who actually resembles your reference images, in roughly the same clothes and setting. If the face drifts, regenerate or add more reference images — more input usually helps consistency.

## Step 4 — Combine footage with a script

The third template, often called **video-to-video** or **script + footage**, lets you feed Kling a short video clip you already have plus a written description of what should change. Think of it as a soft redraw: the AI keeps the general shape and motion of your clip, but re-styles it. Upload a short clip (a few seconds is enough), then type a script describing the new mood, setting, or style. This is the template most people use for stylized social posts — turning a daytime clip into a moody evening scene, for example. Generation takes longer here because the model has more to process.

💬 Example: `Change the setting to a neon-lit Tokyo street at night, keep the same walking motion.`

You'll know it worked when your uploaded clip now looks visually different (new lighting, color, or setting) while the original motion still feels familiar.

## Step 5 — Preview, trim, and export

Once any template finishes, tap the result to open a preview screen. Most flows let you trim the start and end by dragging handles on a small timeline bar. If the clip is too long, shorten it; if the opening is awkward, trim the first second. When it looks right, look for an **Export**, **Save**, or **Download** button — usually at the top or bottom of the preview. On the free plan, you may get a watermark or a lower resolution; higher resolutions and watermark-free exports are typically behind a paid plan. The exact limits change often, so check Picsart's current pricing page if this matters for your project.

💬 Example: trim suggestion — `keep only seconds 2 through 6` (drag the handles until those seconds are highlighted).

You'll know it worked when a finished video file appears in your phone's photo library or downloads folder.

## Common mistakes

- **Uploading a blurry or busy photo.** Kling struggles with tiny faces and cluttered backgrounds. Use the clearest, simplest image you have.
- **Writing prompts that are too long.** Two sentences is plenty. Long paragraphs confuse the model and often produce muddled motion.
- **Expecting perfect hands or text.** AI video still fumbles fingers, writing, and small details. If those matter, plan to crop them out of frame or pick a different shot.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** you can turn a favorite vacation photo into a short clip to share with family, without learning video software.
- **For your business or work:** small businesses can produce quick product clips, social teasers, or stylized B-roll (extra footage used to support a story) without hiring a video editor — useful for one-person shops and busy marketing teams.
- **If you're just getting started:** begin with the photo-to-video template on a single clear selfie or pet photo. It's the fastest way to see what Kling can do in under five minutes.

## Try it now

Open Picsart, search for the photo-to-video template, and upload one clear photo of someone smiling. Type: `The person gently blinks and turns to look out a window, soft natural light.` Tap generate, wait a minute, and watch your first Kling clip come to life.
